items.title: 1.5 Introduction to Hyperbolic and Inverse Hyperbolic Functions

source_refs.note: Book p. 9-10: 1.5 introduction (hyperbolic and inverse hyperbolic functions), printed before 1.5.1

blocks.text: Hyperbolic functions are a class of transcendental functions closely related to exponential functions. They are defined using combinations of \(e^{x}\) and \(e^{-x}\), and their graphs resemble trigonometric functions, although they arise from hyperbolas rather than circles. The basic hyperbolic functions include \(\sinh x\), \(\cosh x\) and \(\tanh x\) which have important applications in mathematics, physics and engineering.

Inverse hyperbolic functions are the inverse functions of hyperbolic functions, defined on suitable restricted domains. They are useful in solving equations involving hyperbolic functions and appear in various applications such as integration, differential equations, and modeling real-world phenomena.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why study them? You already know \(e^{x}\) (section 1.4). The hyperbolic functions are simply two fixed mixtures of \(e^{x}\) and \(e^{-x}\):
\(\sinh x\) uses their difference and \(\cosh x\) uses their sum, each divided by 2. So everything you learnt about \(e^{x}\) (domain \(\mathbb{R}\), always positive, \(e^{0} = 1\), \(e^{x} \to 0\) as \(x \to -\infty\)) is the tool for this whole section.
How to read the names: \(\sinh\) is "hyperbolic sine" (often said "shine"), \(\cosh\) is "hyperbolic cosine" ("cosh"), \(\tanh\) is "hyperbolic tangent" ("than").

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why "hyperbolic"? For trigonometry, the point \((\cos t, \sin t)\) moves on the circle \(x^{2} + y^{2} = 1\). For the new functions, the point \((\cosh t, \sinh t)\) moves on the hyperbola \(x^{2} - y^{2} = 1\). That is the only reason for the name, and it is proved in Example 9 (page 1.5.1).
A real-life picture: a chain or power cable hanging freely between two poles takes the shape of a \(\cosh\) graph (called a catenary).

blocks.title: Teaching note
Key points
blocks.text:
1. Hyperbolic functions are transcendental: they are built from \(e^{x}\) and \(e^{-x}\).
2. Their graphs look a little like trigonometric graphs, but they come from the hyperbola \(x^{2} - y^{2} = 1\), not the circle.
3. The basic ones are \(\sinh x\), \(\cosh x\), \(\tanh x\).
4. Inverse hyperbolic functions exist on suitable (sometimes restricted) domains and are written with \(\ln\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Reading \(\sinh x\) as \(\sin(hx)\) or as \(\sin x \cdot h\): "sinh" is one name, like "sin".
2. Thinking hyperbolic functions are periodic like \(\sin x\): they are not; they are built from exponentials, which never repeat.
3. Writing \(\sinh^{-1} x\) as \(\frac{1}{\sinh x}\): the \(-1\) means the inverse function, not the reciprocal.
